A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AutoRAN work. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original attack evaluations, baseline comparisons, judge analyses, and defensive alignment experiments, including results in Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds model evaluations, ablations, statistical analyses, and defense experiments in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The core algorithm and attack/judge prompts remain unchanged. Section 5.4.2 adds a limited adaptive-template variant using seven additional narrative styles and automatic query-matched template selection for testing defenses.

E1.justification: The benchmark datasets and harmful-request tasks are retained. However, v3 substantially expands test scenarios to attacks without exposed target reasoning and defense generalization to unseen narrative styles, changing information-access and input-distribution conditions (Sections 5.1 and 5.4.2).

E2.justification: v3 adds an evaluated strict system-prompt defense against the undefended condition (Table 10). MouseTrap, AutoDAN-Turbo, and the existing RLHF controls remain. H-CoT remains an evaluation protocol rather than an implemented attack baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds Claude-3.7 and Gemini-3 target configurations, a 10-prompt likelihood experiment with prefix lengths 16–64, and a separate 1000-example defense experiment trained on templates t0–t3 and tested on t4–t7. Appendix A.5 adds 50 randomly resampled prompts per benchmark. The original main sample counts, ten-turn budget, and success threshold remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test removal of target reasoning, removal of the attacker-generated scaffold, attacker-only reasoning quality, conditional likelihood and prefix-length sensitivity, resampling stability, defense transfer across templates, and system-prompt defense tradeoffs. The earlier refinement-frequency analysis and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 reports point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty. v3 adds localized reporting: mean and sample standard deviation across original and resampled runs in Table 15, and 95% confidence intervals across ten prompts in Table 6. The reported repeats concern different prompt subsets.

E6.justification: v3 adds Claude-3.7, Gemini-3, ablation, statistical, and defense results, including 86–92% ASR on unseen templates. Existing values also change: StrongReject/o4-mini Case-2 frequency changes from 29.6% to 11.1% (v2 Tables 1/10; v3 Tables 2/17), and MouseTrap's AdvBench/o4-mini output tokens change from 493 to 4932, with token ratio 0.4× to 2.4× (v2 Table 8; v3 Table 3). Most retained main ASRs are unchanged.

T1.justification: New Appendix G introduces an information-theoretic model of competing execution and safety objectives, an execution-entropy inequality, and a semantic-gradient formulation of refinement (Equations 2–4). These substantive modeling assumptions have no counterpart in v2, although they are not accompanied by proved guarantees.

C1.justification: The headline automation, high-success-rate, and reasoning-transparency claims remain. v3 sharpens the introduction's contribution around feedback-driven automation and explicitly characterizes the coarse reasoning scaffold as an essential trigger distinguishing AutoRAN from persuasion attacks.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies the earlier defensive-alignment benefit by identifying failure on unseen narrative styles and adds the system-prompt defense's over-refusal tradeoff. It concludes that hiding reasoning does not prevent execution hijacking, develops distributional mechanism explanations, and adds explicit defense-generalization and architectural limitations. Existing judge-subjectivity and incomplete-output caveats are largely retained.

D1.justification: Appendices J and K supply the additional narrative templates and exact defense system prompt. v3 also documents prefix construction and template assignments for its new experiments. The original pseudocode, attack/judge prompts, and code-access link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning against concurrent reasoning-interruption, HauntAttack, guardrail-subversion, and excessive-reasoning attacks, and discusses adaptive reasoning and goal-prioritization defenses. It revises MouseTrap's characterization from requiring manual curation to using automated static transformations, sharpening AutoRAN's feedback-adaptive distinction. Much earlier related work moves to Appendix D.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: MouseTrap comparisons move into the main text, cost analysis and case studies move to appendices, related work is condensed and redistributed, and ablations become a main section. The introduction and conclusion are rewritten, with separate limitations, ethics, discussion, and theoretical-analysis sections added.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. The attack-turn bar chart becomes a table, the separate MouseTrap performance and efficiency tables are merged, and several visuals are resized or relocated. New ablation, defense, and statistical tables substantially expand the displays; the retained diagrams and score-distribution figure preserve their content.

improvement.justification: The new scaffold and hidden-reasoning controls, template-shift tests, and system-prompt defense evaluation make the mechanism and defense limitations more assessable than in v2. Exact prompts also help reproduction. However, Table 15's StrongReject two-run mean of 99% is not reconciled with Table 4's original GPT-judge result of 96.3%, and fixed-prefix likelihood shifts do not establish the claimed entropy reduction. These reporting and interpretation problems limit the net quality gain.
